_provenance: Hand-authored from speedrun/ai/source_material.md before any AI generation ran or was looked at. This is the PRD §8 gold set: 50 question/answer pairs used to grade AI-generated and baseline-generated cards against, and to check for leakage into the generation context.

pairs.question: What is another name for the citric acid cycle?
What stage of cellular respiration immediately precedes the citric acid cycle?
What two electron carriers does the citric acid cycle reduce?
Does the citric acid cycle produce most of the ATP from respiration directly?
pairs.answer: No - it produces only a small amount directly; most ATP comes later from oxidative phosphorylation using the NADH/FADH2 it generates.

pairs.question: In which cellular compartment does the citric acid cycle take place?
Which citric acid cycle enzyme is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane rather than dissolved in the matrix?
Why does it make mechanistic sense that the cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix?
pairs.answer: Because the electron transport chain, which uses the cycle's NADH and FADH2, sits on the adjacent inner mitochondrial membrane.

pairs.question: What enzyme complex converts pyruvate into acetyl-CoA?
What are the three products of the link reaction (pyruvate to acetyl-CoA)?
Is the link reaction technically part of the citric acid cycle itself?
pairs.answer: No - it's the required entry step that produces acetyl-CoA, but it is separate from the cycle proper.

pairs.question: What two molecules combine to form citrate in the first step of the cycle?
What enzyme catalyzes the formation of citrate?
What three molecules inhibit citrate synthase?
How many carbons does citrate have?
What enzyme converts citrate to isocitrate?
What intermediate is formed between citrate and isocitrate?
Does the citrate-to-isocitrate isomerization change the carbon count or produce any electron carriers?
pairs.answer: No - it's a structural rearrangement only, with no carbons gained or lost and no NADH/FADH2 produced.

pairs.question: What is produced when isocitrate is converted to alpha-ketoglutarate?
What enzyme catalyzes the first CO2-releasing step of the cycle?
Which enzyme is generally considered the rate-limiting step of the citric acid cycle?
What two molecules allosterically activate isocitrate dehydrogenase?
What molecule is produced when alpha-ketoglutarate is oxidized?
What are the products of the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase reaction?
What other enzyme is alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase structurally and mechanistically similar to?
Name two cofactors shared by alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase.
pairs.answer: Thiamine pyrophosphate and lipoic acid (also FAD, NAD+, and CoA).

pairs.question: What high-energy molecule is produced by substrate-level phosphorylation in the citric acid cycle?
What enzyme converts succinyl-CoA to succinate?
How many steps in the citric acid cycle produce a nucleoside triphosphate via substrate-level phosphorylation?
What electron carrier is reduced when succinate is oxidized to fumarate?
What enzyme oxidizes succinate to fumarate?
What electron transport chain complex is succinate dehydrogenase also known as?
Why is succinate dehydrogenase unique among the citric acid cycle enzymes?
pairs.answer: It is the only one that is physically part of both the citric acid cycle and the electron transport chain.

pairs.question: What enzyme hydrates fumarate to malate?
What molecule is regenerated in the final step of the citric acid cycle?
What is produced when malate is oxidized to oxaloacetate?
pairs.answer: NADH (the cycle's fourth and final NADH of the turn).

pairs.question: Why is the citric acid cycle called a cycle rather than a linear pathway?
pairs.answer: Because oxaloacetate is regenerated at the end and can combine with a new acetyl-CoA to start again.

pairs.question: How many NADH are produced per single turn of the citric acid cycle?
How many FADH2 are produced per single turn of the citric acid cycle?
How many CO2 molecules are released per single turn of the citric acid cycle?
Why does the cycle turn twice per glucose molecule, not once?
pairs.answer: Because glycolysis produces two pyruvate (and therefore two acetyl-CoA) per glucose, each of which drives one turn of the cycle.

pairs.question: Name the three enzymes that are the main regulatory control points of the citric acid cycle.
pairs.answer: Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

pairs.question: What two molecules generally inhibit the citric acid cycle's main regulatory enzymes?
What kind of regulation is this - the pathway's own products suppressing further flux through it?
What does it mean that the citric acid cycle is amphibolic?
pairs.answer: It runs both catabolically (breaking down fuel for energy) and anabolically (supplying precursors for biosynthesis).

pairs.question: Which citric acid cycle intermediate can be exported to the cytoplasm as a precursor for fatty acid synthesis?
Which citric acid cycle intermediate feeds into heme synthesis?
What term describes reactions that replenish citric acid cycle intermediates pulled out for biosynthesis?
What common MCAT misconception involves how much ATP the citric acid cycle directly produces?
pairs.answer: Assuming the cycle directly produces a large amount of ATP, when most of the energy payoff actually comes later from the electron transport chain.

pairs.question: What common net-yield calculation error do students make regarding how many times the cycle turns per glucose?
pairs.answer: Forgetting the cycle turns twice per glucose, not once.

pairs.question: Which two citric acid cycle steps release CO2?
pairs.answer: The isocitrate dehydrogenase step (kc-06) and the alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase step (kc-07).
